newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Czechs drag feet on returning gold, say Slovak Jews.
newsitem.headline: Czechs drag feet on returning gold, say Slovak Jews.

text.p: The Czech National Bank holds gold and precious stones that belonged to Slovak Jews before the Holocaust but seem reluctant to return it, the head of Slovakia's Jewish community said on Wednesday.

"We have placed a completely documented claim with the Czech National Bank, but they haven't come up with an answer," said Jozef Weiss, a Holocaust survivor who is director of the Slovak Union of Jewish Communities.
"We have the whole story, ... fully documented and backed up by eyewitness reports," Weiss told Reuters.

He declined to estimate the amount of gold and valuables which Slovak Jews say are in the Czech central bank's vaults in Prague. But he said it was in the "hundreds of kilos", while the Czechs have conceded it could be around 50 kg (110 pounds).
Weiss is now waiting for a meeting of Czech National Bank (CNB) governors which he hopes will come to a decision on the return of treasure.
"It is difficult to understand why the Czechs are posing problems," he said. "They don't seem to be hurrying."
No one was available for comment at the CNB.
Before World War Two Slovakia, then part of Czechoslovakia, had 70,000 Jews. During the war it became nominally independent under Catholic priest Jozef Tiso, a puppet of Nazi Germany.
The Slovak state paid the Germans 500 marks per head to cover the cost of "removing" Slovak Jews to Nazi extermination camps. Today the community numbers only 3,000.
Weiss said the gold and jewellery belonged to Jews who had been forced to hand it over by the Tiso regime.

The valuables, which were stored in the then Slovak National Bank, were a "deposit" for a 500 million crown "tax" on the Jewish community by the Slovak state. Records show the authorities collected 80,000 pieces of gold and jewellery.
Czechoslovakia was recreated after the Tiso regime collapsed but the country split, this time legally, into separate Czech and Slovak republics on January 1, 1993.
After the war only 4,000 of the 80,000 pieces were returned to Holocaust survivors. The rest stayed in the vaults of what had become the Slovak branch of the Czechoslovak state bank.
In 1953 the treasure was moved to the bank's headquarters in Prague on orders of the communist Finance Ministry.
Each piece was recorded, the gold was melted down, and the precious stones weighed and registered. Gold watches were mostly preserved and are believed to be still in the vaults.
"The records note the carat weight of the stones, which goes into the thousands," Weiss said. The gold was cast into bars and the treasure was added to Czechoslovak reserves.
"It is tragic that the Czechoslovak communist authorities did exactly the same as the Nazis, that is to add the gold stolen from the Jews to the state reserves," Weiss said.
During the split of Czechoslovakia the treasure was not part of the division of property between the two new states, the Slovak government says.

"The Jewish treasure was not included in the split," Slovak Finance Ministry spokeswoman Zuzana Brutenicova told Reuters. "This remains an affair solely between the Slovak Jewish community and the Czech central bank."

Czechoslovakia's gold reserves are still a controversial issue between Prague and Bratislava. But the Prague daily Mlada Fronta Dnes recently quoted a CNB spokesman as saying Czechoslovak central bank gold reserves had been divided in a ratio of 2:1 for the Czech and Slovak republics respectively.
"If this (Jewish) gold was also there, then it was divided in the same ratio," said spokesman Pavel Palivec.
"We want to use this to help the remaining 1,200 or so survivors of the Holocaust," Weiss said. "Time is running out if we are to help them -- most of them are aged over 70."
